1.title: AI Foundations for Governance
1.text: Before we can govern AI, we need to understand it — not as engineers, but well enough to spot risk and ask sharp questions. This module gives you exactly that foundation. Just enough AI to govern it well.

1.title: You Can't Govern a Black Box You Don't Understand
1.text: Here's the good news up front: you do not need to build models to govern them. But you can't treat AI as magic either, because if you do, you'll miss every place risk hides. So we're aiming for the middle path — enough fluency to know what questions to ask, where the risks actually live, and when an engineer's answer doesn't quite add up. Think of this module as learning enough of the language to be dangerous in the right way. Let's build that fluency.

1.title: AI, Machine Learning & Deep Learning
1.text: First, let's untangle three terms people use interchangeably. Artificial intelligence is the broad idea — systems doing tasks that normally need human intelligence. Inside that sits machine learning, which is the key one: systems that learn patterns from data, instead of being explicitly programmed with rules. And inside machine learning sits deep learning, which uses many-layered neural networks and powers today's breakthroughs. They nest, one inside the other. Why does this matter for governance? Because almost all the AI you'll govern is machine learning — which means it learns from data. And that single fact makes the data itself one of your biggest sources of risk.

1.title: How Machines Learn — Three Styles
1.text: Machines learn in three main styles. Supervised learning learns from labeled examples — show it thousands of résumés marked "hired" or "not hired," and it learns to predict the label. This is most business AI. Unsupervised learning finds patterns in data with no labels — like grouping customers into segments. And reinforcement learning learns by trial and error, through reward and penalty — it's behind game-playing systems and is used to tune large language models. Pay attention to supervised learning, because it drives most high-stakes decisions — and here's the catch: it learns by copying patterns in historical labels. So if your history contains bias, the model will faithfully reproduce it.

1.title: Foundation Models — The Shift That Changed Everything
1.text: Now, the shift that changed everything. It used to be: one model, one task. You'd train a spam filter to filter spam, and that's all it did. Narrow. Then came foundation models — a single massive model, pre-trained on a vast sweep of data, that can be adapted to many different tasks. GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama — these are foundation models. Trained once, used everywhere. That generality is incredibly powerful, but it's also a governance headache: when the same underlying model shows up in your chatbot, your search, and your hiring tool, a flaw in that one model propagates everywhere at once.

1.title: Generative AI
1.text: Generative AI is the category of foundation models that create new content — text, images, code, audio, even video. Instead of just classifying or predicting from existing data, it produces something new: a chatbot drafting an email, an image generator making a picture, a coding copilot writing software. And that creative ability is exactly where a brand-new set of risks enters. A model that invents content can invent things that aren't true — that's hallucination. It can reproduce copyrighted material. It can generate convincing fakes. Classic AI never had those problems. Generative AI does, by design.

1.title: Agentic AI — The 2026 Frontier
1.text: And here's where it's heading — the frontier as of 2026. Look at the progression. First we had predictive AI that forecasts. Then generative AI that creates. Now we have agentic AI that plans and acts. An AI agent doesn't just answer your question — it breaks a goal into steps, uses tools, browses, executes actions, and works toward an outcome with much less human involvement at each step. That autonomy is the new governance problem. It's one thing to govern a system that makes a suggestion a human reviews. It's another entirely to govern a system that takes the action itself. Frameworks are scrambling to catch up, and we'll come back to this in Module 10.

1.title: The AI Lifecycle
1.text: Every AI system moves through a lifecycle, and you need to picture all six stages. First, data — collecting and preparing it. Second, train — building the model. Third, validate — testing and evaluating it. Fourth, deploy — putting it into real use. Fifth, monitor — watching it in production. And sixth, retire — decommissioning it when it's done. Here's the governance point: risk enters at every single one of these stages, and so does your opportunity to control it. Bad data in stage one, an untested model in stage three, drift in stage five. Good governance applies across the whole lifecycle — not just a checkbox at launch.

1.title: Provider vs Deployer — A Distinction That Decides Your Duties
1.text: Now one distinction that will come up again and again, because it literally decides your legal obligations. There are two roles. A provider builds or develops the AI system, or places it on the market — think of the vendor who makes the model. A deployer uses an AI system under its own authority — think of Helios using a hiring tool it bought. The EU AI Act, and other laws, assign different obligations to each. And here's what surprises people: most organizations are deployers, not providers — but being a deployer still carries real, enforceable duties. So the very first question to ask about any AI system is: in this case, are we the provider or the deployer?

1.title: The Vocabulary a Governance Pro Must Use Precisely
1.text: Let's lock in the vocabulary, because precision here prevents expensive misunderstandings. A model is the trained mathematical artifact. A system is that model plus everything wrapped around it in real use. Training data is what the model learned from; parameters are the learned values inside it. Inference is the model actually producing an output in use. A prompt is the instruction you give a generative model. Fine-tuning is taking a foundation model and training it further on your specific data. And RAG — retrieval-augmented generation — means grounding the model in your own documents at the moment of the query, instead of retraining it. When legal, risk, and engineering use these words precisely, they put the right controls on the right thing.

1.title: Garbage In, Governance Out
1.text: Let me leave you with the single most important idea in this module. Picture a funnel. Into the top you pour data — and if that data is biased, low quality, or collected without consent, what comes out the bottom is a model that looks authoritative and confident, but quietly encodes every one of those flaws. We say "garbage in, garbage out," but for our purposes it's "garbage in, governance out" — because most AI risk originates in the data: its quality, its representativeness, its provenance, and its consent. That's why, throughout this course, data governance keeps coming back as the foundation.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Let's recap. AI contains machine learning, which contains deep learning — and it learns from data. Supervised learning drives most high-stakes decisions and inherits historical bias. Foundation models led to generative AI, and now agentic AI, each raising the stakes. Govern the whole lifecycle, from data to retirement. Always know whether you're the provider or the deployer. And remember — most risk starts in the data. Next, Module 2: exactly what can go wrong. The AI risk landscape.
